It was a chilly spring afternoon in Tampere, but the Tampere University student cafeteria was buzzing with warm conversations and the clinking of cutlery. As usual, Umar and Arun Kumar, both second-year students in Automation Engineering, had found a quiet spot in the corner to have lunch together.

Umar noticed it immediately.
"Hey Arun, you alright?" Umar asked, looking up from his tray of rice and vegetables. "You seem quiet. Your face looks a bit tense.”
Arun hesitated for a second, then sighed. “Yeah… something’s bothering me. I wasn’t sure if I should say it.”
“Go ahead, bro. I’m listening,” Umar said calmly.
Arun shifted uncomfortably. “Last night, I watched this Indian historical movie — Chhaava. It shows how Aurangzeb, the Mughal emperor, captured and brutally killed Shambaji, the son of Shivaji. It really disturbed me… I mean, those scenes, the cruelty… I couldn’t sleep.”
Umar listened attentively.
“And?” he asked gently.
“I don’t know, Umar. It made me feel… angry. Like, why did Muslim rulers do that to Hindus?”
Umar nodded slowly. He understood where Arun’s feelings were coming from. And more importantly, he knew this was a moment that required patience, not defensiveness.
“I’m really sorry you felt that way, Arun,” Umar said sincerely. “That must’ve been heavy. But can I share something with you, as a friend?”
Arun nodded.
“First of all,” Umar began, “what you saw in the movie is one version of history — maybe accurate, maybe exaggerated. History is complicated, and it’s often written from a certain perspective. Every side tends to show their version in the best light, and their enemies in the worst. We have to be careful not to judge entire communities based on one version of history.”
Arun leaned in, listening more intently now.
“Secondly,” Umar continued, “just because someone was a Muslim ruler doesn’t mean he acted according to Islam. Islam doesn’t allow cruelty or injustice — not even towards animals, let alone humans. If any ruler, whether Muslim or not, committed injustice, Islam doesn't approve of that.”
Arun frowned slightly. “But what about Aurangzeb?”
Umar nodded. “Good question. There are actually historians who say different things about Aurangzeb. Some portray him as a devout and just ruler, others criticize him for being harsh. The truth is — we weren’t there. We can't be 100% sure of everything that happened.”
He paused, then added, “But even if some of the negative stories are true — we as Muslims don’t take Aurangzeb as our role model. Our example is the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his companions, who treated even their enemies with mercy.”
Arun seemed thoughtful. “Hmm... I didn’t know that. I thought Muslims looked up to all the Mughal rulers.”
“Not at all,” Umar replied. “The early caliphs of Islam, like Caliph Umar ibn Al-Khattab, ruled vast empires, but Christians and Jews lived peacefully under their rule. They had rights, safety, and freedom of worship. That’s the Islamic model of governance — not tyranny.”
He continued, “And think about this — if Aurangzeb really wanted to kill all Hindus, would there be so many Hindus still in India today? Why were there Hindu generals under his rule? Why didn’t he kill them?”
Arun blinked. “You’re saying the wars were about power, not religion?”
“Exactly,” said Umar. “Just like Hindu kings also fought other Hindu kings, and sometimes killed each other — it was about kingdoms, territory, and politics. Not faith.”
There was a long silence at the table. The tension in Arun’s face had eased.
“You know,” he said quietly, “I never thought of it like that. Maybe I was quick to judge.”
Umar smiled. “I understand. We all carry some baggage from the media and stories we hear. But we’re in Finland now — far from the noise. And we’ve got this chance to see each other not as stereotypes, but as people.”
Arun nodded slowly. “You’re right. You’ve always been kind and respectful to me. That speaks louder than any movie.”
“And you’ve been a good friend too,” Umar replied. “Let’s not let the past divide the present. Our job now is to build bridges, not walls.”
That day, something shifted between Arun and Umar — not just friendship, but a deeper respect, a shared understanding, and a quiet commitment to see each other as brothers in humanity.
Moral of the story:
We should never judge a whole community based on the actions of some or the way history is portrayed. Real understanding comes from honest conversations, empathy, and the courage to look beyond stereotypes.
